segments.title: Why one published book does not make an established historian
segments.body: Publishing a first monograph is a major achievement, though it does not amount to mastery of the profession. The working benchmark here is roughly three books published and a fourth underway. A new author still depends heavily on exemplary historians, experienced supervisors, and lessons learned during publication. The advice throughout the video therefore comes from an early-career practitioner who is explicit about the limits of his experience.

evidence.note: He calls himself a new author, gives a three-books-plus-one-underway benchmark, and credits Andrew Lambert, Michael Partridge, and Glenn Richardson.

segments.summary: The opening places a first book within a historian's longer apprenticeship, where several completed works are usually needed before an author is treated as established.

segments.title: Finding the historical question a new book can answer
segments.body: Using earlier writing on the Tribal-class destroyers as an example, he distinguishes an admired but lightly sourced ship-by-ship account from a study that tests sources and places a class in its wider institutional and operational setting. The point is not that older books are useless; they can be valuable guides. A new book earns its place by checking the evidence and asking a question the existing literature has not fully answered. His machine-and-cogs comparison shows the difference between collecting individual ship stories and explaining how an entire class functioned within naval policy and operations.

evidence.note: He explains the need for an unsolved story, source checking, and wider context for the Tribal class.

segments.summary: A new history book needs more than a familiar subject: it needs sources and context that let it make a worthwhile contribution.

segments.title: Matching historical communication to an author's strengths
segments.body: For this author, dyslexia makes polished writing slower, particularly within an academic culture shaped by publish-or-perish expectations. That pressure accompanies the precarious progression from contract lecturing towards junior lectureships, fellowships, or postdoctoral work. Public video draws on a skill he finds more natural: speaking directly to an audience. Video still takes time away from books and articles, so it does not replace conventional scholarship. A historian can combine different forms of communication according to individual strengths.

evidence.note: He connects dyslexia, slower writing, publish-or-perish pressures, and the complementary role of spoken history on YouTube.

segments.summary: The discussion of dyslexia and YouTube shows how historians can combine writing with public speaking formats that better suit their individual strengths.

segments.title: Why historians write books
segments.body: For an academic, publication affects professional progression, though people write history for many other reasons. Retirement projects, personal interest, and even a wager can provide the initial motive. Andrew Boyd, for example, pursued major naval-intelligence research once his circumstances gave him the time and security to do so. Financial return is a poor main expectation because the subject must sustain the author through a difficult process.

evidence.note: He discusses personal motives, retired authors, wagers, and money as a poor primary motive.

segments.summary: The video separates career publication, intellectual interest, and personal challenge from the unlikely prospect of easy money.

segments.title: Rejection is part of the publishing path
segments.body: Publication narrows through several stages, with rejection possible at each one. General estimates and the author's own unsuccessful submissions show that a proposal may fail to win a contract, while a contracted manuscript may still never reach publication. Edited collections add another risk because one late or withdrawn contributor can unsettle the whole project. Rejection is common and does not by itself prove that a subject is unworthy.

evidence.note: He gives publication odds, recounts multiple submissions, and describes the fragility of edited books.

segments.summary: A candid account of repeated submissions shows why a promising proposal, and even a contract, does not guarantee a published history book.

segments.title: What publishers mean by a successful first book
segments.body: A history book can be intellectually valuable while still failing its publisher's minimum commercial test. That threshold is selling enough copies to recover the advance and the costs of producing the book. Further levels of success are possible, though this break-even point comes first for a new author. Careful writing and attractive production still cannot control how the market will receive the finished work.

evidence.note: He defines minimum success as sales repaying the advance and the publisher's outlay, then stresses how much reception lies outside the author's control.

segments.summary: The most basic commercial test of a new history book is whether sales repay the publisher's advance and production outlay.

segments.title: Reviews and professional reputation shape a book's reception
segments.body: Neither the author nor the publisher can fully control whether a book succeeds. Sales, reader reviews, and scholarly reviews all influence its commercial and academic reception. A journal review can affect whether other scholars recommend or cite the work, while online ratings can affect discoverability and sales. Public criticism can also have real consequences for colleagues, so a historian with a visible platform should praise generously and avoid casually amplifying disputes.

evidence.note: He discusses sales, journal and online reviews, and the effects of public criticism on historians.

segments.summary: This section weighs sales, journal reviews, and public criticism, stressing the responsibility that comes with a historian's growing audience.

segments.title: Building a research proposal from an earlier question
segments.body: His early projects ranged across the Falklands War, aircraft carriers, amphibious warfare, and the Royal Navy. The successful doctoral proposal expanded an earlier naval-history question into a study of the evolution of naval aviation. A highly polished proposal on the future of naval warfare had already failed, while the less polished naval-aviation idea caught Andrew Lambert's interest. The example shows that a proposal does not succeed only because it is polished: it must offer a compelling research problem and connect with a supervisor who is interested in pursuing it.

evidence.note: He describes undergraduate research, multiple PhD applications, and the proposal on naval aviation that interested Andrew Lambert.

segments.summary: Undergraduate work on naval history became a focused doctoral proposal, showing why a research question and its fit with a supervisor both matter.

segments.title: Disability barriers in postgraduate applications and funding
segments.body: The passage places the mechanics of writing a proposal inside the unequal conditions of postgraduate access. A university telephone process repeatedly ended when the applicant disclosed dyslexia, and the outcomes of a major research-council competition showed a troubling pattern among four colleagues. The account describes those experiences without claiming documentary proof of motive. Searching the full funding list then uncovered a specialist scheme whose eligibility matched his family circumstances, providing an alternative route after the conventional application failed.

evidence.note: He recounts repeated call disconnections after disclosing dyslexia, compares funding outcomes among colleagues, and explains his alternative grant search.

segments.summary: Apparent discrimination around dyslexia during PhD applications and funding leads into an account of how a less obvious eligibility route kept the research possible.

segments.title: Searching widely for research funding
segments.body: An unsuccessful research-council application prompted a search through the full list of less obvious funding opportunities. That search led to the Royal Masonic Trust for Girls and Boys, whose family-based eligibility requirements he met through his father and grandparents. Unusual criteria can deter applicants who assume that a specialist scheme is irrelevant or unattainable. Researchers should read the rules closely and look for a legitimate connection that may make such a fund a better fit than a crowded general competition.

evidence.note: He describes seeking alternative funding and advises students to examine unusual eligible funds.

segments.summary: A funding setback leads to a practical recommendation: examine unusual grants that fit your circumstances, because they may draw fewer applicants.

segments.title: A doctoral thesis is not automatically a publishable book
segments.body: After completing his doctorate, the author withheld the thesis while trying to develop it into a book, then encountered repeated publisher refusals. He returned to journal articles and began looking for a different route forward. A long doctoral argument cannot simply be repackaged unchanged for another publishing form. A dissertation, a journal article, and a trade or academic book each demand a different form of argument and presentation.

evidence.note: He explains withholding the thesis, unsuccessful submissions, and the different demands of journal articles and books.

segments.summary: The move from thesis to book can require years of new proposals, articles, and reframing after publishers decline the original project.

segments.title: Journal articles require a different craft and a long timetable
segments.body: The author's submission record shows how slowly journal publication can move in history. Of twelve articles attempted over his career, only one had appeared by the time of the recording, with three more still pending. Article writing is a distinct craft rather than an easier, shorter version of book writing. The precision and compression that challenge one writer may differ from the qualities that help the same historian sustain a book-length argument.

evidence.note: He gives his article submission and publication numbers, notes long delays, and contrasts article with book writing.

segments.summary: Publication counts and long review delays lead into a distinction between the concentrated craft of an article and the broader strengths needed for a book.

segments.title: History books are built through collaboration
segments.body: Alistair Urquhart coached the author through the distinct craft of journal writing, an example of the reciprocal assistance behind good historical work. Conferences and professional bodies provide places to test ideas, discover sources, and meet people working on related questions. Discussions with peers can redirect research long before the finished argument appears in print. A book may carry one name on the cover, though its research path is often sustained by a wider scholarly community.

evidence.note: He credits colleagues, describes conferences, and calls history a collaborative field.

segments.summary: Behind a single author name are supervisors, colleagues, conferences, and conversations that refine a historical argument.

segments.title: Professional associations connect academic and public historians
segments.body: New-researcher conferences provide recurring places to test ideas for papers and books. The British Commission for Military History includes tour guides and other practitioners alongside university historians. Membership of a national commission does not guarantee that every interpretation is correct, and absence from one does not indicate poor work. Such organizations encourage collaboration and give members a reason to hold themselves to recognizable professional standards.

evidence.note: He discusses new-researcher conferences, national military-history commissions, their varied membership, and their collaborative standards.

segments.summary: The British Commission for Military History illustrates how conferences and associations can link academics, guides, and independent researchers around shared standards.

segments.title: How mentors and editors help a book reach publication
segments.body: The account of meeting an editor through Andrew Lambert illustrates the value of trusted academic networks. It also avoids reducing publication to connections alone: the author still faced a contract, a delayed schedule, disrupted research, and the need to adapt working habits during the pandemic. Moving from quiet external workplaces to writing at home required a deliberate change in routine and eventually a separate garden office. Support can create an opportunity, but a book emerges only through sustained work after that introduction.

evidence.note: He describes an introduction to a Pen and Sword editor, the contract timeline, pandemic disruption, and adapting his writing routine.

segments.summary: A supervisor's introduction can open a conversation with an editor, but the author still has to complete the research and writing.

segments.title: Budgeting for an archive-based history book
segments.body: The book required an estimated £16,000 of personal investment, and more than half of that had been spent before the publishing contract was signed. When teaching contracts arrived late or were cancelled, keeping the project moving eventually meant carrying about £6,000 in credit-card debt. A first-book advance will not normally cover costs on that scale. Archive visits require travel, accommodation, food, and time away from paid employment. The practical advice is to budget conservatively and include a much larger contingency than feels necessary because delays and changing circumstances are common.

evidence.note: He details personal spending, limited advances, archive travel, and the risks of insufficient contingency.

segments.summary: Research travel, time away from paid work, and unexpected delays make a history book a substantial personal financial commitment.

segments.title: The overlooked costs of research travel and illustrations
segments.body: Research for the book involved archives at Tyne and Wear, Woolwich, Greenwich, Chatham, Portsmouth, Plymouth, Yeovilton, Falmouth, Cambridge, and the National Archives at Kew. Each visit brings costs for transport, accommodation, food, equipment, and time away from paid work. Booking a train well in advance can make first-class travel only slightly more expensive while including food, a power socket, and a usable place to work. For longer stays, a midweek hotel package may offer better value than a budget room when it includes meals, secure equipment storage, parking, and suitable working space. Publication rights for historical photographs can also be expensive, while cover artists and professional indexers need paying for their labour. Outsourcing the index was a disability-related quality-control choice because anxiety about a missed entry would make self-indexing disproportionately costly. These expenses explain why a polished illustrated history is not cost-free to produce.

evidence.note: He covers archive-trip logistics, equipment security, photograph rights, cover art, indexing, and professional advice.

segments.summary: Travel planning, safe working conditions, image rights, cover art, and indexing all affect the practical cost of producing a history book.

segments.title: Photograph rights and cover art belong in a book budget
segments.body: Archive research does not automatically provide the right to reproduce every image found there. Imperial War Museum licensing could have added a large expense, while access to Drachinifel's private collection reduced the cost of illustrating this book. The cover creates a separate obligation because commissioned artists must be paid for their work. Image permissions and creative labour belong in the publication budget rather than being treated as free decoration.

evidence.note: He describes the expense of photograph reproduction rights, help from Drachinifel's collection, and the need to pay cover artists.

segments.summary: The cost of an illustrated history includes permission to reproduce photographs and fair payment for the artist who creates its cover.

segments.title: Why professional indexing was an accessibility decision
segments.body: Some authors compile their own indexes, but that option was poorly suited to these circumstances. The concern was less an inevitable indexing error than the prolonged anxiety that one might have been missed. Fear of dyslexia-related mistakes can reduce sleep and concentration, creating the conditions for the very mistakes the author wants to avoid. Hiring a professional indexer therefore served as both quality control and a practical disability accommodation.

evidence.note: He explains why he outsourced the index and how anxiety about dyslexia-related errors can damage sleep and increase the risk of mistakes.

segments.summary: Paying a professional indexer protected the book's quality and the wellbeing of a dyslexic author.

segments.title: Protecting the value of historical expertise in media work
segments.body: Ordinary scholarly generosity differs from commercial media work that depends on expert labor. Students may spend hours briefing television researchers and sending written material without arranging payment or a firm role in the programme. An agent can establish that research, consulting, and speaking have value before the historian commits substantial time. Although this author has no literary agent for books, he relies on experienced advice when contracts or legal wording need scrutiny.

evidence.note: He recommends representation for television work, describes unpaid researcher calls, and contrasts that with his access to contract advice.

segments.summary: Advice about agents and television researchers warns historians not to give hours of specialist research away on the vague promise of future exposure.

segments.title: Why a second history book can still be speculative
segments.body: A planned five-per-cent contingency became a 40 to 45 per cent overrun after ordinary setbacks and pandemic disruption. For the next project, the editor offered extensive advice but no advance because the proposal remained speculative. A supportive publisher or supervisor can open a door, yet the historian still has to produce the research that justifies a contract. Planned visits to archives in Glasgow and at Kew would have to begin while travel restrictions and access remained uncertain. Reception of the first book would also affect the author's leverage when proposing the second. Early-career authors therefore need to distinguish encouragement from a firm commitment and budget for research that may never lead to publication.

evidence.note: He contrasts a five-per-cent contingency with a 40 to 45 per cent overrun, calls the next book speculative, and describes the research and sales evidence needed before a contract.

segments.summary: A first publication does not remove financial uncertainty: the next book may remain speculative until months of archival work show that a contract is viable.

segments.title: How an author's track record changes publishing leverage
segments.body: A publisher may express interest, ask for more research, and still decline the project after the historian has spent the time and money. That risk distinguishes new authors from established writers with several successful books and veteran figures whose reputations let them complete a manuscript before offering it. Norman Friedman, Andrew Lambert, Nicholas Rodger, and Andrew Boyd illustrate the far end of that professional spectrum. Senior authors may still face rejection, though a proven audience and record shift more of the uncertainty away from the writer.

evidence.note: He describes publishers withdrawing after preliminary research and contrasts new, established, and veteran authors.

segments.summary: The contrast between new, established, and veteran authors explains why early-career historians may have to fund research before a publisher will commit.

segments.title: Redefining a sustainable career in history
segments.body: A permanent academic post remains an ambition, but years of applications and an interview rate of roughly one in eight show the emotional cost of making it the only measure of success. YouTube also does more than publicize finished work because viewers send articles, research leads, and personal contacts that can enrich future projects. Patreon and merchandise income provide a modest but predictable fund for archive days, allowing a contract lecturer to decline some teaching hours without resorting to credit-card debt. Books, occasional university teaching, public video, and television work can reinforce one another. This mixed career differs from the tenure-track future first imagined, yet it can still support a meaningful living in history.

evidence.note: He discusses the mental-health cost of repeated job applications, research leads and income from his audience, archive time, teaching, books, video, television, and a mixed history career.

segments.summary: After years of academic job applications and repeated rejection, books, teaching, public history, television work, and audience support offer another route to a viable career without a permanent university post.

segments.title: How a public audience can strengthen archival research
segments.body: The online audience acts as a distributed research network whose members send old papers, local knowledge, and contacts with relevant experience. Those contributions can reveal evidence or people that a historian working alone might never encounter. Patreon and merchandise income also create a small but predictable fund that can replace some contract-teaching hours with days in the archives. Public history can feed back into academic research through information, relationships, and time, even when the audience is not enormous.

evidence.note: He describes viewers sending papers and contacts, then explains how recurring audience income lets him trade some teaching hours for archive research.

segments.summary: Viewer knowledge and modest recurring support can supply both new research leads and protected time for archive visits.
